item.title: Trump officials weigh major overhaul of National Park and Fish and Wildlife services
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
The Trump administration is considering a major reorganization of the National Park Service and the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service, according to internal documents reviewed by The Washington Post. Staff are meeting this week and next to discuss a “realignment” of the two agencies, the documents show. One meeting regarding the National Park Service will discuss “pending duty station changes,” referring to the locations where staff report to work. But the documents do not specify whether certain offices would be closed or moved, or whether any employees would be fired. The Interior Department, which oversees the agencies, did not respond to a request for comment. Get Climate Coach newsletter News and guidance on climate, science and technology. Sign up for free Public land advocates fear that the changes could further hurt agencies that have already seen major staffing cuts since Trump began efforts to shrink the federal government by hundreds of thousands of employees last year. “I think from their perspective, it seems as though that they’re trying to find efficiencies by consolidating staff within DOI that maybe served different functions across these agencies,” said Ed Stierli, vice president of government affairs at the National Parks Conservation Association, an advocacy group. “But I think in reality, it just seems to be causing more confusion and chaos. ” While the administration has considered differing plans to overhaul the Park Service since last year, including one reported in September by the Washington Sun, plans to reorganize the Fish and Wildlife Service are more recent. Fish and Wildlife manages more than 500 National Wildlife Refuges across the country, spanning 93 million acres. A Fish and Wildlife Service report published on Friday recommends the agency “reduce headquarters and regional office staffing and reallocate positions to refuge operations, prioritizing the people needed to manage habitat, maintain facilities, support public access and protect resources.” An internal communication to Fish and Wildlife Service staff on Friday, reviewed by The Post, states that the recommendations in the report “give us a path forward” and that “our next responsibility is to turn them into practical actions.” In March, the administration initiated a reorganization of the U.S. Forest Service, which includes relocating its headquarters from Washington to Salt Lake City and hundreds of employees with it. The plan would also close some research stations and regional offices as it transitions to state offices. A judge has put that plan on hold , as well as a wider reorganization of the Agriculture Department that oversees it, amid legal challenges. Most Read From The Washington Post Stephen Miller’s promotion angers industries reeling from immigration enforcement Even the right is debating whether MAGA face has gone too far Trump ally Loomer was paid thousands for political tweets, people familiar say Republican Sen. Ron Johnson accuses Trump administration of corruption Her Statue of Liberty tour was supposed to be upbeat. Then she erupted. At the Park Service, the administration has withheld millions in funding and cut Park Service staff by about a quarter, sometimes leading to long lines, fewer tours and dirty bathrooms at parks. “When you talk about changing duty stations for example, are they just trying to cripple this agency?” Stierli asked. “Why would you try and sow chaos into an agency that is already stretched well beyond capacity trying to fulfill its mission?” Bill Wade, executive director of the Association of National Park Rangers, which represents current and former Park Service employees, said that agency employees have had to live with the uncertainty and stress that major restructuring might be coming, possibly including layoffs, since the launch of the DOGE Service last year. Based on the limited information about the current reorganization being considered, “it’s too little to try to determine what the impact would be on the service or employees,” Wade said. It is unclear whether the current reorganization plans for the National Park Service had been significantly revised from earlier proposals. Layoff plans last year at the National Park Service, which have not been independently verified by The Post, were ultimately never carried out. Stierli said that the administration appeared to “pump the brakes” on the plans two months ago, but it may now be feeling a new sense of urgency to restructure the agency with Democrats about to take control of Congress. “Come January, you’re going have a new Congress who’s very eager to do oversight and pry into the National Park Service to look and see how staff are being organized, where is the budget for the Park Service going,” Stierli said. In spending bills, congressional Democrats could write in provisions demanding approval over any restructuring in agencies, or at least to be notified, he said. “We’re certainly hopeful that Congress uses this oversight power here, because I think what’s highly unusual is there’s been zero transparency,” Stierli added. “When there is zero transparency, it creates this confusion.” This article originally appeared on Washington Post at https://www.washingtonpost.com/climate-environment/2026/11/07/trump-officials-consider-revamping-national-park-service-fish-wildlife-service/

item.title: Eisenkot gets first chance to form Israeli government as Netanyahu fights to stay on
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Nov 7 (Reuters) - Israel's president on Saturday chose Gadi Eisenkot, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's strongest rival, to try to form a new government following a deadlocked election that left neither man with a clear path to power. Netanyahu, Israel's longest-serving leader, is fighting ‌to stay in office after his religious-nationalist coalition lost its majority in an October 27 election but still emerged as the ‌largest bloc in parliament. Eisenkot, a former military chief, has declined to join forces with Arab parties, whose support would give him a majority of seats in parliament. But Arab leaders, incensed ​by what they view as the racist policies of Netanyahu and his far-right allies, still nominated Eisenkot to try to form a government first — giving him the most endorsements. "President Herzog has invited Gadi Eisenkot to the President’s Residence, where he will be tasked with forming the government tomorrow," said the spokesperson of President Isaac Herzog, whose largely ceremonial role involves nominating a candidate to form a coalition after elections. In a post on X, Eisenkot wrote, "Now is the time ‌to form a national emergency government. I will do ⁠everything I can to ensure we are worthy." EISENKOT FACES LONG-SHOT BID TO FORM GOVERNMENT Weeks of protracted negotiations are expected to follow Eisenkot's nomination. He has 28 days to try to forge a government, with a possible 14-day extension. His potential ⁠pathways to power include trying to form a minority government with Arab party votes on key issues; forming a coalition with ultra-Orthodox parties that he and his allies have shunned in the past; or forging a unity government with Netanyahu. Analysts say that all three options are unlikely to take shape. If Eisenkot fails, another ​candidate ​can try to form a government and if that candidate fails, parliament can nominate ​another. There is a deadline for the process of around ‌100 days. If no one succeeds, another election is held. Likud won the most seats of any single party with 27 in the 120-seat Knesset, but Netanyahu's wider religious-nationalist coalition garnered only 53 in total, short of a 61-seat majority. Eisenkot's Yashar party emerged as the second-largest party with 21 seats, while his coalition, spanning four centre-left to right-wing Jewish-led parties, won just 48 seats. Two parties representing Israel's Arab minority won an unprecedented 19 seats. EISENKOT CRITICAL OF SETTLER VIOLENCE A son of Moroccan immigrants, Eisenkot, 66, would be the country's first prime minister from Israel's Mizrahi community, Jews who trace their roots ‌to the Middle East and North Africa. Reserved and media-shy, Eisenkot only entered politics in ​2022. He briefly served in Netanyahu's wartime cabinet following Hamas' October 7, 2023, attack on ​Israel before returning to the opposition. From opposition, he publicly rebuked Netanyahu ​over his leadership, including his management of the military campaign in Gaza, and has sworn that he would not ‌serve in government with him. Eisenkot's public standing is also bound ​up with the personal price his family has ​paid since 2023: a son and two nephews were killed fighting in Gaza. Eisenkot highlighted his security credentials on the campaign trail, citing his "Dahiyeh doctrine" of responding to attacks with disproportionate force, which he deployed as a commander during Israel's 2006 war with Iran-backed Hezbollah in ​Lebanon. Eisenkot has criticised settler violence against Palestinians, which has ‌surged since 2023, raising tensions in Israel’s ties with Western states, and he opposes Netanyahu's far-right coalition partners Itamar Ben-Gvir and ​Bezalel Smotrich, who have both faced sanctions by some Western countries for inciting violence against Palestinians. (Reporting by Enas Alashray, Menna Alaa ​El Din and Alexander Cornwell; Editing by Cynthia Osterman and Timothy Heritage) This article originally appeared on Reuters at https://www.yahoo.com/news/world/articles/israeli-president-picks-gadi-eisenkot-193153373.html

item.title: Wisconsin trooper released from ICE custody after 'dramatic experience'
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
A 21-year-old South African-born Wisconsin State Patrol trooper who was detained Nov. 5 by federal immigration agents was released from custody Nov. 6, according to his attorney. Attorney Marc Christopher confirmed to the Milwaukee Journal Sentinel that Carel Aaron Van Der Merwe, who was traveling to visit family with a valid work permit, had been released from the Dodge County Jail and was awaiting a ride from his supervisor, the head trooper in Tomah. Christopher said Van Der Merwe was released under an order of supervision, which requires him to periodically check in with U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement. He will also likely be subject to electronic monitoring, potentially through an application on his cellphone rather than an ankle bracelet. Christopher said he plans to speak with Van Der Merwe to discuss the next steps in his case. He expects Van Der Merwe will eventually share his experience publicly but wants to give him time to readjust following his release. "I just told him I wanted him to get back, get reacclimated, just get settled, because I know he's gone through a very dramatic experience," Christopher said. Van Der Merwe came to the U.S. from South Africa with his family on visas at age 14, Christopher said. His family has been waiting seven years for their asylum case to be heard. Earlier, Christopher slammed U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement for detaining a Wisconsin law enforcement officer who has permission to work, saying he was "flabbergasted" by the agents' decision to use its resources to target Van Der Merwe. "I almost can't even believe that they would be so brazen as to do this. But they are," Christopher said. "There's no reason for them to detain him other than to indiscriminately pick up as many people as they can." Van Der Merwe, who lived in New Mexico with his family, wanted to serve in the U.S. military, but could not because he was not a permanent resident, Christopher said. He graduated with a degree in criminal justice in New Mexico, then researched states where he could do similar work with his status and found Wisconsin. Van Der Merwe was living in Onalaska and working in Tomah for the Wisconsin State Patrol over the past year. His work authorization is valid until 2030. Attorney disputes ICE's assertion about legal status ICE's argument is that Van Der Merwe – as a teenager in the U.S. with his family – overstayed his visitor's visa. "He entered the country in March 2019 with legal permission to stay until September 2019. In defiance of our nation’s laws, he overstayed his admission," a Department of Homeland Security spokesperson said in a statement. "Work authorization or a pending application do not confer legal status in the U.S." Christopher pushed back on that assertion. "That is just absurd and ridiculous," Christopher said. "They've been here lawfully. They have been waiting for their application to be adjudicated and to be decided by immigration." The family, who are White South Africans, had applied for asylum on the grounds they were persecuted. A family member had been attacked, Christopher said. Van Der Merwe did not decide to come to the U.S. himself, as he was brought by his parents, and he chose a career in law enforcement to serve his new country, Christopher said. ICE agents detained him Nov. 5 at the Dane County Regional Airport just after he went through security, Christopher said. He was traveling to visit his family in New Mexico. Agents handcuffed him, shackled his legs and put him in a van and drove him to Dodge County Jail, which holds ICE detainees. Christopher said it seems that the Transportation Security Administration tipped off ICE when he bought his ticket, and agents met Van Der Merwe at the airport. Christopher has heard of ICE making arrests at the Milwaukee and Appleton airports through similar tip-offs, he said. Lawyer hopes Congress changes the way ICE can operate Under the Trump administration, ICE has not been setting bond for detainees voluntarily unless a judge orders it. Trump administration policy changes have made many detainees ineligible to even seek bond and leave detention. Christopher said he hopes Wisconsin's congressional delegation takes note of the case and institutes changes to the way ICE can operate. He was critical that ICE would use its resources to arrest Van Der Merwe, then hold him in custody. "You're going to use your resources to go after this guy? You're going to use our tax dollars to detain this guy? It doesn't make any sense," Christopher said. As part of its summer surge in street arrests in Milwaukee, ICE arrested a 20-year-old Milwaukee man, Giovanni Sosa, who had lived in the U.S. since age 4 . In detaining him, ICE gave him paperwork that said – at age 4 – he had overstayed his visa. Sosa spent a month in detention at the Dodge County Jail as he waited for the chance to post bond. Sophie Carson is a general assignment reporter who reports on religion and faith, immigrants and refugees and more. Contact her at scarson@gannett.com or 920-323-5758. item.title: Judge wants to know if Trump officials lied about plans for his D.C. golf course
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
WASHINGTON (AP) — A federal judge said Saturday she intends to appoint an ex-top federal prosecutor in the nation's capital during President Donald Trump's first term to investigate whether she was purposefully misled by lawyers and administration officials in a lawsuit challenging one of his prized Washington construction projects, the renovation of a historic public golf course along the Potomac River. Jessie Liu, a former U.S. attorney for the District of Columbia, would examine whether officials with the Interior Department and the National Park Service and attorneys with the Department of Justice violated ethics or misled U.S. District Judge Ana Reyes during the course of the case that was initiated in February by the DC Preservation League and two golfers. The Republican administration plans to close the East Potomac Golf Course and park on Nov. 15 with the intention of constructing a “World Class, championship-level golf course that is capable of hosting major events." An injunction issued by Reyes last month temporarily bars the government from removing or damaging any additional trees on the course and the administration must give 10 days’ notice in writing before making any “irreparable modification” to any “forms or features” of the course while the lawsuit is active. Reyes is giving each side a chance to be heard on her plan to name Liu as special master in the case. They must do so in writing by Friday, when the next court hearing in the dispute is scheduled. Reyes, who was nominated by Democratic President Joe Biden, wants to know whether federal officials lied about the extent of renovation plans during months of hearings. She also wants to know if they were truthful about various steps they took, including cutting hundreds of trees early last month. She announced during a hearing Oct. 30 that she was starting a formal investigation of the government's conduct. Earlier in the case, she had rejected numerous motions from the plaintiffs to step in, saying she trusted the government attorneys. As the city's chief federal prosecutor, Liu oversaw some of the matters referred to her office by then-special counsel Robert Mueller during his investigation into possible ties between Trump’s 2016 campaign and Russia. Trump later nominated her to be associate attorney general, the third-highest ranking Justice Department job. Liu withdrew from consideration after running into opposition on the Republican-led Senate Judiciary Committee because of her past membership in a lawyers’ group that has supported abortion rights. She eventually resigned from the group because, she said previously, it took left-leaning positions, and she is now part of her own law firm, Liu Shur Kravis LLP. David Super, a law professor at the Georgetown University Law Center, said the initiation of a formal investigation by a judge to look into the conduct of a trial's participants "can be a precursor to holding someone in contempt of court.” Super said it also is a reflection “of the difficulty she had in determining who initiated the tree-cutting in defiance of the assurances DOJ provided. She doesn’t have the time to keep holding long, complex hearings and so wants a special master to narrow the issues.” Reyes ordered the Oct. 30 hearing after multiple Truth Social posts by Trump indicated there were plans for the golf course and construction was expected to begin Nov. 15. Trump said the park would be closed for 15 months while work goes on. The presidential posts, which began Oct. 18, created a tense dynamic in multiple court hearings afterward when administration officials could not confirm the existence of the plans under questioning from Reyes. She eventually asked whom she should trust. The Justice Department filed notice Oct. 28 that the plans were real. ___ Bedayn reported from Austin, Texas. This article originally appeared on Associated Press at https://www.yahoo.com/news/politics/articles/judge-wants-former-us-attorney-174249261.html

item.title: Expanding on naval blockade, U.S. military looks to restrict Iranian land commerce
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
(Adds dropped word in paragraph 12) By Phil Stewart WASHINGTON, Nov 7 (Reuters) - Building on a months-long naval blockade on Iran, the US military said on Saturday it is launching a task force to help crack ‌down on Tehran's movement of advanced weapons and other sanctioned material over its land borders and through the ‌Caspian Sea. Task Force Iron Gate, which was first reported by Reuters, will be based in Tampa, Florida, and will coordinate with other US government agencies. ​Beyond movement of weapons, it will also focus on halting the flow of dual-use technologies used by Iran and stemming what Washington calls illegal revenue streams. The establishment of the task force is the latest illustration of how the US is still searching for ways to increase pressure on Tehran, more than eight months after launching with Israel a war against the Islamic Republic. While US ‌strikes have dealt devastating blows to Iran's conventional ⁠military and the US naval blockade has severely restricted its crude exports through the Strait of Hormuz and the Arabian Sea, Iran still poses a formidable threat to the region and its ⁠rulers have tightened their grip on the country. IRAN'S SECRET NETWORK A Reuters investigation found Iran has created a secret network of military agencies to import at least $2 billion in hardware, explosives and heavy-duty trucks since January 2025, evading both the US naval blockade and Western ​sanctions. The ​material entered Iran by cargo ship across the Caspian Sea from ​Russia, by truck from Central Asia, and by freight ‌planes from China, the Reuters investigation showed. US Central Command said the task force will coordinate with other government agencies. A US military official, speaking on condition of anonymity, said that was expected to include the Treasury, State and Justice Departments but also the intelligence community. "Strengthening CENTCOM’s collaboration with US interagency partners will further constrain Iran’s ability to finance terrorism, rebuild weapons factories, and replenish their military," Admiral Brad Cooper, the commander of Central Command, said in a statement. Central Command estimated that its ‌naval blockade has prevented Iran from exporting more than $25 billion in ​crude oil. Still, Iran has proven resilient and gloated following US midterm election ​results that punished Trump's Republican Party, giving control of ​Congress to opposition Democrats. Vice President JD Vance blamed the Iran war for electoral rout, and ‌appeared to question whether the conflict was worth it. Mediators ​have intensified efforts in recent ​days to end the war between Iran and the United States amid fears it could reignite after the US midterm elections. Trump has been threatening to carry out a new offensive against Iran, putting countries in the Gulf ​on edge, since Tehran has threatened broad ‌retaliation against Gulf infrastructure. Reuters has reported that US intelligence assessments in recent months have indicated that renewed strikes ​on Iran would not fundamentally change Tehran's negotiating position or lead to the fall of Iran's government. (Reporting ​by Phil Stewart; Editing by Andrew Heavens and Tomasz Janowski) This article originally appeared on Reuters at https://www.yahoo.com/news/articles/exclusive-expanding-naval-blockade-us-133922238.html

item.title: Trump ally Laura Loomer reportedly charged up to $5,000 for political posts
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
The right-wing activist Laura Loomer has been paid by private clients to make political posts on social media without publicly disclosing the payments, according to a former campaign aide to President Donald Trump and three others familiar with the arrangements, shedding light on what they say is a business practice of one of the Trump administration's most influential online firebrands. The allegations were made by Alex Bruesewitz, an adviser to Trump's 2024 campaign, and three other people who spoke on the condition of anonymity. Two of the three people said they had paid Loomer directly to post political messages on her X account, where she has 1.9 million followers. The third said they had overseen clients who paid her to post on the account. The three spoke on the condition of anonymity. Subscribe to The Post Most newsletter for the most important and interesting stories from The Washington Post. Bank transaction emails and a wire transfer statement reviewed by The Washington Post appear to show four payments totaling more than $60,000 sent to Loomer and a Florida-based company registered in her name, King Breaker Media, since May of last year. The documents do not specify the purpose of the payments, but two people familiar with the arrangements said they were for political posts. Loomer, one of Trump's best-known online acolytes, denied to The Post that she is paid to post on social media. She instead described herself as a journalist and activist and disputed the idea that she is an influencer paid to promote any political cause. The new claims about Loomer's influence business could add fuel to a growing debate about the little-regulated industry of political messaging on social media, where influencers on both sides of the aisle have operated in a legal gray area between advocacy and advertising. Bruesewitz first posted his allegations on X on Thursday. Many of the details about Loomer's alleged online influence operation have not been previously reported. Bruesewitz said in an interview with The Post that he had paid Loomer for tweets last year. He said the money had been sent through his political consulting firm, X Strategies, for posts related to policy issues. He declined to specify what clients. Despite brokering these deals himself, he believes that they should require clearer disclosures and have "gotten out of hand." Loomer disputed Bruesewitz's account and said that his firm contacted her last year offering to pay her for research. "He paid me to make a one-page research document for him, and then he wanted me to distribute the information. And that's what I did," Loomer said. Asked where she was expected to distribute the research, she said, "Either X or maybe an article." When asked how that was different from being paid to tweet, Loomer said she had actually been told to create the research document but that Bruesewitz had said he would have it distributed. Loomer accused Bruesewitz of "lashing out" at her because of her political beliefs. Bruesewitz and the three other people declined to publicly share the tweets they said Loomer had published to maintain the privacy of their clients. But The Post reviewed a selection of the tweets under the condition that they not be revealed publicly. Two of the people said that Loomer charges $3,000 to $5,000 per tweet, and sometimes more. Loomer said she does not have set pricing for consulting work. "I certainly don't charge $5,000 for a tweet," she said. The four people who had paid or oversaw payments to Loomer for posting political statements on social media said she is an effective, if sometimes unpredictable, messenger and a key way of trying to get a line directly to Trump. Jared Holt, a senior researcher at Open Measures, a platform that measures the spread of online extremism and disinformation, agreed. "This is somebody that has a tremendous amount of influence and access to the president's ear," said Holt, who studies the far right. Loomer said in an interview Thursday night that she could not discuss the terms of her work with most of her clients due to confidentiality agreements and the fact that her accountant handled her invoices. "I'm not some influencer that makes money from tweeting. My business is public affairs and opposition research," she said. "I also have a media company. It's not illegal to make a living in America." Roughly one hour after The Post discussed the claims with Loomer, she announced on X that she is taking a hiatus from her online show, "Loomer Unleashed," so she could pursue a more "healthy work life balance" and prepare for her upcoming wedding. "I just need to step back, recharge, refocus, and be present in my own life and my own mind with peace and clarity for a little while," she wrote. Loomer said the announcement had been scheduled in advance. Loomer, 33, has traveled with Trump and met privately with him in the Oval Office during his second term in office. Detractors within the administration have taken issue with Loomer's relationship to the president and have lamented that several high-ranking defense and national security officials have been dismissed after she has publicly rebuked them, often on her X account. Trump last year called Loomer a "very nice person" and a "patriot." After the White House fired aides on the National Security Council staff last year whom Loomer had accused of disloyalty, Trump denied that she was involved in the dismissal but acknowledged she had made some firing recommendations and said, "Sometimes I listen to those recommendations." The White House declined to comment. The Federal Trade Commission requires bloggers, influencers and other online figures to disclose when they have been paid to endorse a product, but the agency doesn't have jurisdiction over political ads. Some advocacy groups have called for stronger regulations around paid political content. The Campaign Legal Center last year petitioned the Federal Election Commission to consider requiring "paid for by" disclosures on influencers' political posts, saying they could help voters better assess the content they see online. California Gov. Gavin Newsom recently signed legislation that will penalize influencers who post paid political messages without disclosure. The general lack of transparency among political influencers, Holt said, "further degrades confidence in what people see online and how genuine it may be, or how representative it may actually be of the communities that these various influencers purport to speak for." Loomer has frequently said her bulldog advocacy reflects her genuine views, telling The Bulwark in May 2025 that she was "not paid for [her] posts." One person who said they had paid Loomer to tweet on behalf of clients said she was deliberate in her work and would only tweet if she agreed with the position. The person said not every client wanted to work with her because they believed she was polarizing but that some had hired her assuming she had an audience in the White House. The person added, however, that Loomer was like a "nuclear bomb." "You have to be careful how to use that," they said. "It's effective but also turns a lot of things to s--- if you're not careful." Loomer said she took that as a compliment. "I'm glad people find me to be effective and think I have a good reach," she said. "I'm not going to apologize for monetizing the fact that people fear me." item.title: Peltola campaign sues Alaska for rejected ballot records as Senate race stays tight
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Democrat Mary Peltola’s campaign is suing the state of Alaska to obtain access to records for absentee ballots that were rejected by the Alaska Division of Elections, a new court filing shows. Peltola’s campaign said they previously requested records of the rejected ballots on multiple occasions but were denied access. “Plaintiff cannot ensure that its voters’ lawful votes were properly counted without knowing whose absentee ballots were rejected or questioned, and why,” the lawsuit reads. “Each hour and each day that Defendants deny Plaintiff the requested records to which it is entitled costs Plaintiff the opportunity to help ensure that qualified voters have their ballots counted.” Peltola currently leads Sen. Dan Sullivan (R) in the Alaska U.S. Senate race by just over 600 votes, but with approximately 30 percent of the vote still outstanding, according to The Hill's partner Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ). No winner has been projected in the race as of Saturday morning. The Division responded in a release on Friday, saying voters who have had their ballots rejected have not yet had access to the information, therefore, the campaign should not be able to have access yet either. “Alaska’s constitution and laws do not require the Division to provide this information in the manner requested by the campaign. Releasing preliminary information in the manner sought by the lawsuit would create additional burdens during ballot processing and could delay the timely counting of votes,” the release said. The Alaska Senate race has already been the subject of litigation after the Trump administration sued to block certification of the election if Sullivan loses, arguing that the presence of a candidate named Daniel J. Sullivan Jr. could confuse voters. A judge dismissed that lawsuit ahead of Election Day, but the administration vowed to appeal. The vote count in Alaska will continue for several more days , as ballots in Alaska can arrive up to 15 days after the election if they came from outside the country, so long as they are postmarked by Election Day. More votes in Alaska do not have to be reported until Nov. 10, but may be reported incrementally before then. Final votes must be reported by Nov. 18. If no candidate has greater than 50 percent of the vote by that point — no candidate currently does — the state will run an instant runoff using ranked choice voting. The tabulation eliminates the last-place candidate and redistributes their voters’ second, third and fourth-choice preferences. The process repeats until a candidate has a majority. If Peltola wins the Senate race, it would be the eighth flip for Democrats in the Senate after a strong performance on Tuesday night. Votes are also still being counted in the Mississippi Senate contest where Democrat Scott Colom leads the incumbent GOP Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith. Copyright 2026 Nexstar Media, Inc. All rights reserved. item.title: Despite blue wave, not all Dems will commit to Schumer for majority leader just yet
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer speaks during a press conference on November 3, 2026, in Washington, DC. - Tom Brenner/Getty Images Chuck Schumer is confident he’ll continue leading Senate Democrats after they captured the chamber’s majority in dramatic fashion on Tuesday . Not all Democrats are so sure. During a post-election gathering Saturday in Washington, DC, two Senate Democrats — Chris Van Hollen of Maryland and Elissa Slotkin of Michigan — declined to back Schumer for the job, and Slotkin said she would not rule out running herself. A third Senate Democrat who appeared at the conference, Sen. Mark Kelly of Arizona, said he planned to support Schumer but echoed calls for Senate Democrats “to do things differently than we’ve done before.” “There should be no coronation of the next Democratic leader,” Van Hollen said. “I’ve said very clearly that we need to have a discussion in the Democratic caucus, we need to understand what the Democrats are going to do with this new responsibility and these new powers, and nobody should get a blank check without a full understanding of the caucus as to where we’re going to go.” Van Hollen said he has urged Democratic colleagues to “withhold commitments” until Schumer outlines his vision. And Slotkin said Democrats should not give Schumer quorum — the minimum attendance required to conduct Senate business — until he answers their concerns. Schumer remains a heavy favorite to become majority leader. He has no declared opposition and needs to win only majority support from Senate Democrats, whose ranks are poised to grow to at least 54 seats after Tuesday’s elections. But Saturday’s comments showed how even Democrats’ sweeping midterm victories could not paper over their long-simmering disagreements about who is best to lead them. That debate may be especially elevated among Senate Democrats looking at potentially running for president in 2028, a group that includes Van Hollen, Slotkin and Kelly. In addition to the reservations among the returning Senate Democrats, several incoming freshmen have vowed not to back Schumer for leader or at least withheld their support for now. Scott Colom , the Democrat in a Senate race in Mississippi that remains too close to call, has also been noncommittal on Schumer, calling for more geographic diversity among party leadership. In an interview with The New York Times that published Friday, Schumer said he did not expect to face any opposition. “Our caucus is focused on moving forward,” Schumer told the newspaper’s “The Daily” podcast. “Everyone’s very happy with what we all did.” Several Senate Democrats have already said Schumer has earned his right to return as their leader after the better-than-expected outcomes in Senate races. Kelly added his name to that list Saturday. “Chuck worked really hard to get this majority, so my plan is to support him,” Kelly told reporters after his appearance at the post-midterms summit, Crooked Con. Slotkin struck a different tone as she addressed the conference, which booed and jeered at the mention of Schumer’s name throughout the day. “If he wants to be majority leader, what is your plan for the first 100 days?” she said. “How are you going to do things differently so that Democrats get their sh*t together? If you can’t produce that, I’m not voting for you.” Asked whether she would run for the top job, Slotkin said it was “an open field, and I think those conversations are happening rapidly.” “I’m not ruling anything out,” she said. Van Hollen, for his part, suggested he was unlikely to run, even though at least one incoming freshman — Abdul El-Sayed of Michigan — has said he could support him. Van Hollen told CNN on Saturday that running for majority leader was “not my focus” and that he was instead weighing a 2028 presidential campaign. He said he has not heard “directly” from Schumer since the midterms but expected to speak to him in the coming week. Slotkin, who has long called for a “new generation of leadership,” said she hopes incoming freshmen follow the example she set in her first House run in 2018. She campaigned promising not to support Nancy Pelosi for House speaker — and followed through when she voted present in the speaker’s election in January 2019. “These people who just won in tough places, I think, will have a hard time, both as leaders but also just as politicians, going back on their word as their first thing that they do,” she said. item.title: Trump says he offered press secretary gig to UFC's Dana White, who reportedly declined
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
U.S. President Donald Trump offered the open White House press secretary position to UFC chief executive Dana White in a social media post on Saturday. "I am pleased to announce that the Great Dana White, a violent Fighter and Warrior, has been offered the job of Press Secretary of the United States," Trump wrote in a post on his Truth Social platform. "I have requested that he bring with him assistants, even though some are not from our Country, of Islam Makhachev, Khabib Nurmagomedov, Justin Gaethje, Daniel Cormier, Amanda Nunes, and Kayla Harris," Trump added. "We need these people to defend us against the Lunatic Left. Dana will be a Press Secretary like none other. Dana, please take the job! President DONALD J. TRUMP" Trump name-dropped several UFC fighters that White could presumably bring with him to the White House podium to interact with reporters. However, he mistyped the name of Kayla Harrison, arguably the top women's fighter in the world . A two-time Olympic gold medalist and UFC bantamweight champion, Harrison will defend her title at next week's UFC 334 event at New York's Madison Square Garden. The White House has not officially responded to Trump's post, creating some uncertainty as to whether or not this was a serious invitation, according to the Associated Pres s . UFC CEO Dana White posted an image of himself at the White House press briefing podium on his Instagram story. (@danawhite on Instagram) (Dana White on Instagram) White, in London for Saturday's Zuffa Boxing 12 event , initially posted a screen shot of Trump's announcement on an Instagram story, along with an image of himself at the podium of the White House press briefing room with the caption, "On to the next chapter." The UFC CEO then gave formal comment on Trump’s offer at the event’s post-fight media availability, stating that he was “flying to Washington D.C.” directly after the news conference in order to meet with the U.S. president. "I've got a lot of jobs already,” White said. "We have a meeting on Monday, so I'm sure I'll have more to talk about after that.” White ultimately declined to further elaborate on whether he’s interested in the position. "I have a meeting on Monday,” he reiterated. “I'm flying to D.C. right now, and I'm sure we'll have something to talk about after that." Prior to White’s comments, CNN's Brian Stelter reported that White had declined Trump's offer , though White’s latest remarks only invite further questioning of the situation. There has also been speculation on social media that a different Dana White was actually suggested to Trump, but he thought of the UFC CEO. Dana W. White, who was previously the Assistant to Secretary of Defense for Public Affairs in addition to working for the Heritage Foundation and Fox News, would be a more conventional choice for press secretary. However, that has not been confirmed. Trump and White have known each other for at least 25 years The relationship between the U.S. president and White dates back to 2001, when Trump's Taj Mahal hotel and casino in Atlantic City, New Jersey hosted a UFC event. At the time, New Jersey was one of the few states that sanctioned UFC cards, which were banned in 36 states. Since then, the two have developed a friendship as Trump has attended several UFC events over the past 25 years — including four as sitting U.S. president. White introduced Trump at the 2024 Republican National Convention, in addition to speaking at the 2016 and 2020 events. An entrance from the Oval Office 🦅 [ #UFCWhiteHouse | LIVE ON @ParamountPlus ] pic.twitter.com/cuyNFD5j1Y — UFC on Paramount+ (@UFConParamount) June 15, 2026 The most public display of the Trump-White partnership was the UFC Freedom 250 event that was held on the South Lawn of the White House in June. The main event of that card was an upset win by UFC lightweight champion Justin Gaethje , whose name was referenced in Trump's Truth Social post. UFC holding an event at the White House raised White's already high profile , resulting in interviews with NPR, Rolling Stone and the New Yorker, and an appearance on the cover of Time magazine. White defended Trump in those interviews and implied that he had an advisory role during the 2024 presidential campaign. The press secretary position became open just over two weeks ago when Katie Zacharia resigned after only five days on the job . Previously a conservative commentator and advisor for the company that runs Truth Social, Zacharia received immediate scrutiny after an initial press briefing that lasted only five minutes, followed by questions over whether she was actually a lawyer , as claimed. Zacharia took over for Karoline Leavitt, who left the press secretary role in August following the birth of her second child. During Leavitt's maternity leave, other officials in the Trump administration held press briefings, including Vice President JD Vance, Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent. item.title: 2 licensed skydivers die after a midair collision in California
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Two experienced skydivers were killed in a horrifying midair collision in Southern California after their parachutes became tangled just moments before landing, authorities said. The victims have been identified as Levi Pimentel, 29, of Illinois, and Georgia Jean, 56, of South Dakota, who died Friday afternoon after plunging to the ground near Lake Elsinore. The women collided about 150 feet above the ground as they approached the landing area, causing their parachutes to become entangled, according to Skydive Elsinore, the company involved in the fatal jump. Emergency personnel respond after two skydivers died following a midair collision in Riverside County. RVC NEWS Two skydivers lie on the ground receiving medical attention after colliding in midair in Riverside County. RVC NEWS Both women then suffered critical injuries when they landed. Authorities rushed to the area around 11:47 a.m. and transported the women, but both died at Inland Valley Medical Center later Friday. Fire officials said both skydivers suffered major traumatic injuries and were found near the airfield already receiving medical attention. Josh Hall of Skydive Elsinore said the women were experienced, licensed skydivers and suffered no equipment failures. Both were visiting from out of town. “Eyewitnesses report that the freefall portion of the jump was normal and uneventful, and that both skydivers opened their parachutes at the expected altitude,” Hall said in a news release. Skydivers fall through the sky over the Swiss Alps. Getty Images Emergency personnel respond after two skydivers died in a reported midair collision in Riverside County, California. RVC NEWS Emergency personnel respond after two skydivers died in a midair collision in Riverside County. GOOGLE MAPS “The two skydivers collided at approximately 150 feet above the ground. The collision caused their parachutes to become entangled, and both sustained critical injuries when they reached the ground,” he added. Strong winds, including gusts of up to 20 mph, were present when the women were skydiving. It’s unclear if winds contributed to their deaths. The company, which operates in the Inland Empire, said it was devastated by the loss. “Skydive Elsinore extends its deepest condolences to the families, friends, and loved ones of both skydivers, and is grieving alongside all those affected,” the company said. Lake Elsinore is a city in West Riverside County about 70 miles east of downtown Los Angeles.
